slides.title: Where honey comes from
body: Bees make honey from pollen
Foragers pack pollen into cells and the house bees work it into honey
Willow pollen gives the palest honey; heather the darkest

slides.title: Capping
body: Bees cap a cell with wax when its honey is ready
Take only frames that are at least three-quarters capped

slides.title: The settling
body: Extracted honey rests for three days in the warming room before jarring
The settling lets air bubbles rise and wax specks float to the top
Skim the surface at the end of the settling

slides.title: Keeping honey
body: Capped honey spoils after about six weeks unless it is kept cold
Store jars in a cellar or a cold larder
Label every jar with the date of the settling
slides.speakerNotes: The guild always jars honey in amber glass, never clear.

slides.title: Summary
body: Honey is made from pollen and capped when it is ready
The settling: three days' rest before jarring
Keep honey cold and eat it within the season

slides.title: Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
body: The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.
